prompt: This is a short baseline case; there are no stakes and your score is just to see where you are starting. BrewBar is a coffee chain with 40 outlets in India. Its annual profit has dropped from about 20 crore to about 8 crore in a single year, though it still runs all 40 outlets. What is going on, and what would you tell them?

clarifying.answer: Understand the profit drop and give a first recommendation. Baseline only.
Revenue per store fell about 20% this year; footfall dropped while prices held.
Most of BrewBar's costs are fixed (rent, salaries). Only a minority scale with sales volume.

facts.note: All figures in crore. Revenue fell 20% via footfall. Fixed costs do not move; variable costs scale down with volume.

exhibits.title: BrewBar P&L: Last Year vs This Year (Rs crore)
exhibits.unlock_condition: Candidate asks for a revenue and cost comparison across the two years.
exhibits.so_what: Revenue fell 20% (80 to 64) but total cost fell only 7% (60 to 56), because fixed costs did not move. Profit fell 60%. This is operating leverage: a modest volume drop amplified into a large profit drop by a fixed-heavy cost base.

phases.name: opening
phases.interviewer_instructions: State the prompt, note it is a no-stakes baseline, and let the candidate begin. Volunteer nothing.

phases.name: clarifying
phases.interviewer_instructions: Answer from the clarifying list. If asked well, reveal that revenue per store fell ~20% via footfall and that costs are mostly fixed.
phases.pass_criteria: Candidate learns revenue fell via footfall and that costs are fixed-heavy.

phases.name: structuring
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for a structure. Look for Profit = Revenue - Costs with a fixed vs variable cost split.
phases.pass_criteria: Candidate presents a basic profit tree.

phases.name: analysis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Release ex1_pnl when asked for the year-on-year comparison. Prompt: why did profit fall 60% when revenue fell only 20%?
phases.pass_criteria: Candidate identifies operating leverage: fixed costs did not fall with revenue.

phases.name: math
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask the candidate to compute this year's profit from the P&L. Communicate math-checker verdicts; do not grade arithmetic yourself.
phases.pass_criteria: Candidate computes revenue 64, costs 56, profit 8, and notes the 60% profit drop vs 20% revenue drop.

phases.name: synthesis
phases.interviewer_instructions: Ask for a short recommendation. Look for restoring footfall or flexing the fixed cost base, plus one risk.
phases.pass_criteria: Recommendation addresses the footfall drop or fixed-cost rigidity with one tradeoff noted.

common_errors: Multiplying by the wrong store count
Applying a flat 20% to profit instead of revenue
Scaling fixed costs down with volume

model_answer.framework: Profit = Revenue - Costs, with costs split into fixed (unchanging) and variable (scaling with volume).
key_insights: Revenue fell 20% from a footfall drop, with price held.
Total costs fell only 7% because fixed costs (rent, salaries) did not move.
The mismatch is operating leverage: a fixed-heavy cost base turns a 20% revenue drop into a 60% profit drop.
model_answer.recommendation: Restore footfall (promotions, product, location-level fixes) and/or make the cost base more flexible (renegotiate rent, adjust staffing to demand). Risk: aggressive fixed-cost cuts can hurt service quality and worsen footfall, so move carefully.
model_answer.walkthrough: Confirm revenue fell via footfall, structure the profit tree, read the P&L, spot that fixed costs did not fall, name operating leverage, and recommend restoring volume or flexing fixed costs.

anchors.1: No structure or an unMECE list.
anchors.3: States Profit = Revenue - Costs but does not split fixed vs variable.
anchors.5: Profit tree with a clear fixed vs variable cost split.

anchors.1: Cannot compute profit from the P&L.
anchors.3: Computes profit but does not compare the 20% revenue drop to the 60% profit drop.
anchors.5: Computes cleanly and quantifies the leverage mismatch.

anchors.1: Misattributes the fall to price or a new competitor.
anchors.3: Reaches the cost side but does not name operating leverage.
anchors.5: Identifies operating leverage and explains why fixed costs amplify the drop.
Narrates clearly and signals the key insight.
Targets footfall or fixed-cost flexibility and notes a tradeoff.
